title: Sound: where it comes from and how it reaches our ears
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 1 Physics: Where do sounds come from? (Unit 6.1) and Sounds move (Unit 6.3), plus hearing, ears, echoes and animal hearing. No textbook needed.
summary: Every sound starts with something vibrating, which means shaking very fast. Your child feels their voice box buzz, makes rice jump on a bowl drum and builds a string telephone. They find that sound travels through air, water, wood and string, and gets quieter further away. They also meet elephants who feel low rumbles through their feet, and tomato plants that click when they are thirsty.
builds_on: This is the first lesson on sound. In Class 5 your child comes back to it to learn about loud and quiet sounds (volume), high and low sounds (pitch), and fair tests.
subconcepts: every sound is a vibration (shaking very fast)
our voice box vibrates when we talk and sing
how the ear catches sound: outer ear, eardrum, brain
sounds get quieter as they travel away from the source
sound spreads out like ripples in a pond (a wave)
sound travels through air, water, wood and string
no air, no sound: sound needs something to travel through
protecting our ears from very loud sounds
animals hear sounds we can't (elephant rumbles, bat squeaks)
listening with the body: feeling sound through feet and hands
goals: By the end your child can name ten sound sources at home and outside, made by people, animals, machines and nature.
By the end your child can show that a sound comes from something shaking, using rice on a drum or a hand on their throat.
By the end your child can say that sound travels to our ears, and gets quieter the further it goes.
By the end your child can show that sound travels through string and wood as well as air.
By the end your child can say why we cover our ears for very loud sounds, and how some animals hear sounds we cannot.
By the end your child can say one thing scientists still do not know about sound and animals.
words: what we hear with our ears
the thing that makes a sound
to shake very fast, backwards and forwards
a big sound that is easy to hear
a small, soft sound that is hard to hear
the part of our body that catches sound
a thin skin inside the ear that shakes when sound arrives
a sound that bounces off a wall or hill and comes back
the part in your throat that buzzes when you talk

days.title: Sounds all around us
days.goal: Notice sounds and their sources, and meet the story.

steps.title: One minute of listening
steps.do: Set a phone timer for one minute. Sit together with your eyes closed. Say: 'Count every different sound you hear on your fingers.' Then ask: 'What did you hear? Where did it come from?' Good answers: the fan, the pressure cooker, a crow, a scooter horn, a neighbour talking, your own breathing. Say: 'Anything that makes a sound is called a sound source.'

steps.title: Story: Lakhi Listens with Her Feet
steps.do: Read the story aloud slowly. Use a low, rumbly voice for Grandmother. Don't explain it. Then ask: 'How did Lakhi find her family when she could not see them?' and 'Why did Grandmother say stand still?' Remember your child's answers. You will come back to them on Day 3.

steps.title: Sound source hunt
steps.do: Fold a sheet of paper into four boxes: People, Animals, Machines, Nature. Walk through the house and out to the balcony or the gate. Each time your child hears a sound, they draw its source in the right box, or you write it. Aim for ten. Ask: 'Which sound was loudest? Which was quietest? Which source could you not see?' Start the Sound diary (activity a1) on the back of the sheet.

need: a sheet of paper and a pencil

days.title: Every sound is a shake
days.goal: Feel and see that sounds come from vibrations.

steps.title: Bee breath and the buzzing throat
steps.do: Start with Bhramari, the humming bee breath from yoga. Sit tall and close your eyes. Press the small flap at the front of each ear closed with a finger. Breathe in through the nose. Breathe out with a long, low 'mmmm', like a bee. Do it three times. Ask: 'Where did you feel the hum?' Good answers: the head, the face, the teeth or the chest. Then your child puts their fingertips on the front of their throat. They say 'aaah', then hum, then whisper, then stay silent. Ask: 'When did you feel a buzz?' Good answer: a strong buzz when talking or humming, very little when whispering, nothing when silent. Say: 'Inside your throat is your voice box. When you hum, it shakes very fast. Shaking very fast is called vibrating. Every sound starts with something vibrating.'

steps.title: Dancing rice
steps.do: Do experiment e1. Stretch cling film tightly over a steel bowl. Put a pinch of uncooked rice on top. Ask: 'What will happen to the rice if I bang a steel plate just above the bowl? Why do you think so?' Wait for the guess. First tap the cling film with a finger. Then bang the plate with a spoon just above the bowl. Watch the rice jump. Then twang a rubber band stretched over an open tiffin, and watch it blur. Say: 'The plate vibrates. It pushes the air, and the air pushes the cling film. That is how sound reaches your ear too.'

steps.title: What's shaking?
steps.do: Look at the sound hunt sheet from Day 1. For each source, ask: 'What is vibrating to make that sound?' Help with answers. A horn has a thin metal plate inside that vibrates. A crow's voice box vibrates. Leaves rub and shake against each other. If you are stuck, tap a steel glass with a spoon. Your child touches the glass gently and feels the buzz. Then hold the glass tight. Ask: 'What happened to the sound?' Good answer: it stopped, because the glass stopped vibrating.

need: a rubber band and an open box or tiffin

days.title: How we hear
days.goal: Understand that the ear catches the shaking air, and that other animals hear differently.

steps.title: Bigger ears
steps.do: Do experiment e2. Your child stands three big steps away, with their back to you. Rub your fingers together softly. Then they cup their hands behind their ears and listen again. Then they hold a paper cone with the narrow end near the ear, never inside it. Ask: 'When was it easiest to hear?' Then ask: 'A rabbit must hear a dog or a fox creeping up. How do their tall ears help them?' Good answer: big ears catch more sound, and a rabbit can turn each ear towards a noise.

steps.title: Inside the ear
steps.do: Draw a simple ear: the outer ear like a funnel, a tube going in, and a thin skin across the end of the tube. Say: 'This thin skin is the eardrum. When sound reaches it, the eardrum vibrates, like the cling film on our drum. Tiny bones pass the vibration on. Then a nerve carries a message to the brain. We hear with our ears and our brain together.' Then say clearly: 'Never put anything inside your ear, not even a finger or a cotton bud. The eardrum is thin and can be hurt.'

steps.title: Elephants who hear low
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v1. Katy Payne, a scientist in the USA, stood near the elephants at a zoo. She felt a throbbing in the air but heard nothing. She found that elephants call to each other with rumbles too low for people to hear. Remind your child of Lakhi in the story. Ask: 'How could you find out if an animal can hear a sound that you can't hear?' Good answers: play the sound and watch whether the animal turns their head or comes closer, or use a machine that records the sound. Then ask: 'Dogs hear many quiet sounds that we miss. How might that help a dog?'

need: a sheet of paper for a cone

days.title: Loud and quiet, near and far
days.goal: Find out that sounds get quieter as they travel away, and learn to protect our ears.

steps.title: Walk-away test
steps.do: Do experiment e3 in a long corridor, or along the longest path through your home. Stand still and rub your fingers together softly, the same way each time. Your child walks away one big step at a time and says 'still hear it' after each step. Where they can't hear it any more, put a chappal. Then tap a spoon on a steel glass, the same way each time, and do it again. Mark that spot with a second chappal. Ask first: 'Which sound will you hear from further away? Why?' Afterwards ask: 'What happened to the sounds as you walked away?' Good answer: both got quieter. The tap was louder, so it could be heard further away.

steps.title: Too loud!
steps.do: Ask: 'Which sounds are so loud that they hurt? What do you do?' Good answers: crackers, a big speaker at a wedding, a loud horn. Say: 'Very loud sounds can harm the tiny parts inside the ear. That harm does not get better. So we cover our ears and move away, and we keep headphones quiet.' Ask: 'How do you think a dog or a bird feels on a night of crackers?'

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1 together. Read each item aloud and let your child point or say the answer while you mark it. For the two 'why' items, write down exactly what your child says.

need: a steel glass and a spoon
two chappals to mark the spots

days.title: Sound travels through things
days.goal: Show that sound travels through string, wood and water, but not through empty space.

steps.title: String telephone
steps.do: Do activity a2. A grown-up makes a small hole in the bottom of two paper cups with a pencil. Push a 5-metre string through and tie a big knot inside each cup. Walk apart until the string is tight. Talk softly into one cup while your child holds the other cup to their ear. Then let the string go loose and try again. Then pinch the string in the middle. Ask: 'When did it work best? What happened when we pinched it?' Good answer: a tight string carries the vibration. Pinching stops the vibration, so the sound stops.

steps.title: Ear on the table
steps.do: Your child puts one ear flat on a wooden table. Scratch the far end very lightly with a fingernail. Then they lift their head, and you scratch the same way again. Ask: 'When was the scratch louder?' Good answer: with the ear on the table. Say: 'Sound travels through wood better than through air. It travels through water too. That is how fish hear underwater.'

steps.title: A bell in a jar with no air
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v2. About 350 years ago in England, Robert Boyle put a ticking watch inside a glass jar. His helper, Robert Hooke, had built a pump to take the air out. As the air went out, the ticking got fainter and fainter. Ask: 'Why do you think the ticking got fainter?' Good answer: sound needs air, or something else, to travel through. Ask: 'There is no air in space. Would a blast in space make a bang?' Good answer: no, it would be silent. Then ask the voice question.

days.title: Echoes and secret listeners
days.goal: Hear echoes, think about plants that click, and play the sound game.

steps.title: Echo hunt
steps.do: Go to a staircase, an empty room or a corridor with hard walls. Clap once, sharply, and listen. Ask: 'Did the clap ring or come back?' Say: 'That is an echo. The sound bounced off the hard walls and came back to you, like a ball bouncing off a wall. In a small space it comes back so fast that it mixes with the clap and sounds like ringing.' Ask: 'Will a clap echo in a room full of cushions and curtains?' Try it. Good answer: much less, because soft things soak up sound. Say: 'Bats find their way in the dark by making high squeaks and listening for the echoes.'

steps.title: Do plants make sounds?
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v3. Scientists in Israel put tomato plants in quiet boxes with special microphones. The plants made tiny clicks, too high for people to hear. Thirsty plants clicked far more often. Ask: 'Who might be listening to a thirsty plant? A moth? Another plant?' Then ask the voice question. Say: 'Nobody knows yet whether any animal listens to these clicks. Maybe you will find out one day.'

steps.title: Sound Trail board game
steps.do: Play the board game g1. Before starting, read the rules aloud. When a player lands on a sound square, they must make that sound or say what is vibrating. Play until someone reaches HOME, or for 14 minutes.

days.title: Make music, dance the shake
days.goal: Use music, dance, water and drawing to feel that sound is a shake that spreads.

steps.title: Ripples like sound
steps.do: Fill a wide steel plate or basin with water and wait until the water is still. Your child taps the middle of the water once with a fingertip. Ask: 'What do you see?' Good answer: rings of ripples spread out and get fainter. Then tap the rim with a spoon and watch tiny ripples shiver across. Say: 'Sound spreads out from its source like these ripples, in every direction. A vibration that travels like this is called a wave. The water stays in the plate. Only the wave travels. As the rings get bigger, each part of them gets weaker. That is why a sound gets quieter far away.'

steps.title: Kitchen orchestra
steps.do: Collect a steel glass, a steel plate, a wooden spoon, an empty plastic bottle, a tin with dry rice in it, and a pot with a lid. Your child taps, shakes or rubs each one and says what is vibrating. Good answers: the metal, the wood, the rice hitting the tin. Then make a short piece together: four quiet taps on the bottle, four loud bangs on the pot, one rice shake, then silence. Play it once loud and once quiet. Ask: 'Which one rang the longest? How did you stop it?' Good answer: touch it, so it stops vibrating. Last, clap a rhythm and let your child copy it. Then swap.

steps.title: The shake-and-freeze dance
steps.do: Play any song. While it plays, your child shakes like a sound: small, fast shakes for a mosquito's whine, big, slow wobbles for a big drum. When you stop the music, they freeze: no vibration, no sound. Then the family stands in a line holding hands. The first person wiggles and passes the wiggle down the line. Ask: 'Did anyone walk to the end of the line? What travelled?' Good answer: only the wiggle travelled. Sound travels through air in the same way.

steps.title: Portraits of sound
steps.do: Give your child crayons and paper. Say: 'Draw what a sound looks like, using only lines.' Ask for three drawings: a crow's caw, rain on the roof and Amma's lullaby. Spiky, wavy, dotted, thick or thin: there is no right answer. Ask: 'Why did you choose those lines for the lullaby?' Write your child's words under each drawing. Keep them for the sound map.

need: a wide steel plate or basin of water
a steel glass, steel plate, wooden spoon, plastic bottle, tin with rice, pot with lid

days.title: Sound map, check and teach it back
days.goal: Finish the sound map project, review and teach the family.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2 together. Read each item aloud. For the 'why' and 'how could you test' items, ask your child to explain while you write their words.

steps.title: Finish the sound map
steps.do: Finish the project. On the map of your home, your child draws a small picture of each sound source in its room, like the cooker in the kitchen and the fan in the bedroom. Loud sounds are red and quiet sounds are blue. Ask: 'Which room is the noisiest? Which is the best quiet place to read?'

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child shows the family the dancing rice and the string telephone. They explain three things. Sounds come from vibrating things. The vibration travels through air, string and wood to our ears. Sounds get quieter far away. Then ask the check questions aloud. Praise every answer that uses the word 'vibrate'.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Try three items from Worksheet ws3 today, especially 'Would a drum make a sound on the Moon?' Do the rest tomorrow if your child enjoys it. Write down exactly what your child says.

need: the dancing rice bowl and string telephone

experiments.title: Dancing rice
experiments.question: Do sounds come from something shaking?
need: a rubber band and an open tiffin or box
steps: Stretch cling film tightly over the bowl like a drum skin.
Sprinkle a few grains of rice on top.
Tap the cling film gently with a finger. Watch the rice.
Hold the steel plate just above the bowl and bang it hard with the spoon. Watch the rice.
Stretch the rubber band over the open tiffin and twang it. Look at the band closely: does it look blurry?
Touch the twanging band. What happens to the sound?
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: 'Will the rice move if we bang the plate without touching the bowl? Why do you think so?'
experiments.observe: The rice jumps when you tap the cling film. It also jiggles a little when you bang the plate just above it. The rubber band looks blurry while it vibrates. When you touch it, the vibrating and the sound stop together.
experiments.why: Sound is made when something vibrates. The banged plate pushes the air next to it back and forth. That air pushes the air next to it, all the way to the cling film. The cling film vibrates too and throws the rice up. Stop the vibrating and you stop the sound.
experiments.safety: Bang gently so the noise does not hurt anyone's ears. Keep the rice away from very young siblings.

experiments.title: Bigger ears
experiments.question: Do bigger ears help us hear quiet sounds?
need: a sheet of paper rolled into a cone and taped
steps: Your child stands three big steps away with their back to you.
Rub your fingers together or crinkle a paper softly. Ask: 'Can you hear it?'
Now your child cups their hands behind their ears, palms forward. Make the same sound.
Now they hold the cone with the narrow end near their ear (not inside it). Make the same sound.
Swap: you listen while your child makes the sound.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which will help most: nothing, cupped hands or the cone?'
experiments.observe: The sound seems louder with cupped hands, and often louder still with the cone pointed at the sound.
experiments.why: The outer ear works like a funnel. It catches sound and sends it into the ear. A bigger funnel catches more sound, so a quiet sound seems louder. A rabbit has to hear a dog or a fox creeping up in time to run. Their tall ears catch more sound, and they can turn each ear towards a noise.
experiments.safety: Never push the cone or anything else into the ear.

experiments.title: Walk-away test
experiments.question: What happens to a sound as it travels further away?
need: a steel glass and a spoon
two chappals to mark the spots
a long corridor, or the longest path through your home
steps: Stand still at one end of the corridor.
Rub your fingers together softly, the same way each time.
Your child walks away one big step at a time and says 'still hear it' after each step.
Where they can't hear it any more, put a chappal.
Now tap the spoon on the steel glass, the same way each time, and do the same again. Mark that spot with the second chappal.
If your child reaches the end and can still hear the tap, mark the end. That sound goes further than your corridor.
Count the steps to each chappal.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which sound will you hear from further away: the finger rub or the spoon on the glass? Why do you think so?'
experiments.observe: Both sounds get quieter as your child walks away. The finger rub fades after only a few steps. The spoon tap can be heard much further away.
experiments.why: A sound spreads out in every direction, like ripples from a stone in a pond. The further it goes, the more it spreads, so it gets weaker and sounds quieter. A louder sound starts with a bigger vibration, so it can travel further before it is too weak to hear.
experiments.safety: Do this indoors or in a corridor, away from roads and stairs.

activities.title: Sound diary
need: the back of the sound hunt sheet
steps: Each evening this week, sit quietly for one minute.
Draw or say one new sound you heard that day and what made it.
Put a star next to sounds made by animals and a circle next to sounds made by machines.
At the end of the week, count: more stars or more circles?
activities.outcome: A week's diary of sounds, and a question: is our home full of animal sounds or machine sounds?

activities.title: String telephone
need: a pencil to make the holes
steps: A grown-up makes a small hole in the bottom of each cup with a pencil.
Push the string through each hole and tie a big knot inside.
Walk apart until the string is tight.
One person talks softly into a cup. The other holds their cup to their ear.
Try with the string loose, then tight, then pinched in the middle, then wrapped round a chair leg.
activities.outcome: A working telephone, and the discovery that sound travels along a tight string.

voices.idea: In 1984, Katy Payne stood near the elephants at a zoo in Portland, in the USA. She felt a throbbing in the air, like standing near a big organ pipe, but heard nothing. She and her team recorded the elephants. They found the elephants were calling to each other with rumbles too low for people to hear. These sounds are called infrasound, and they can travel for kilometres.
voices.then: Katy Payne had already studied whale songs with her husband, Roger Payne. Other scientists were convinced once the recordings showed the low calls.
voices.now: It is accepted: elephants talk in very low rumbles, and later scientists such as Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell found that they may also feel these rumbles through the ground with their feet and trunks.
voices.ask: Katy Payne noticed a feeling that no one else had paid attention to. How could you find out if an animal can hear a sound you can't hear?

voices.who: Robert Boyle (1627–1691) and Robert Hooke (1635–1703), England
voices.idea: In 1660 Boyle reported putting a ticking watch inside a glass jar and pumping the air out. The ticking grew fainter and fainter, and came back when air was let in. The air pump that made this possible was built by his assistant, Robert Hooke.
voices.then: In the 1640s in Rome, Gasparo Berti rang a bell inside a tube with the air taken out, and still heard it. Athanasius Kircher, who wrote about the test, said that sound does not need air. The sound had probably escaped through the metal that held the bell, and some air may have been left inside. Boyle's careful test convinced most people that sound needs air, or something else, to travel through.
voices.now: It is accepted: sound needs something to travel through (air, water, wood). In empty space there is no sound. Hooke, the skilled builder whose pump made the test possible, became a great scientist himself but is often left out of the story.
voices.ask: Kircher said one thing and Boyle said the opposite. Why might two careful people get different results? What would you need to check?

voices.who: Itzhak Khait, Lilach Hadany and colleagues, Tel Aviv University, Israel (published 2023)
voices.idea: They put tomato and tobacco plants in quiet boxes with special microphones. They recorded tiny clicks, too high for people to hear. The plants clicked far more often when they were thirsty or when their stems were cut. A computer could tell a thirsty plant from a cut one by their clicks.
voices.then: Many scientists were amazed. Others pointed out that the clicks are probably caused by tiny air bubbles in the plant's water tubes, so the plant may not be 'talking' on purpose.
voices.now: The recordings are accepted, but what they mean is debated. Nobody knows yet whether any animal, such as a moth looking for a healthy plant to lay eggs on, actually listens to them.
voices.ask: If a plant clicks without meaning to, could the click still tell an animal something? What experiment would show whether a moth listens?

project.title: Sound map of my home
steps: Draw a simple map of your home: one box for each room, plus the balcony or yard.
Spend a few minutes in each room and listen.
Draw a small picture of each sound source in the room where you heard it.
Colour loud sounds red and quiet sounds blue.
Find the quietest spot in the home and mark it with a star: that is your listening spot.
Stick your three sound portraits on the map next to the rooms where you hear those sounds.
project.outcome: A coloured sound map of the home, with the noisiest and quietest places found.

game.title: Sound Trail
rules: Put all counters on START. Take turns to roll the die and move.
If you land on a sound square, make that sound and say what is vibrating to make it. If you can, move on 1 square.
If you land on a 'forward' or 'back' square, do what it says.
The first player to reach HOME wins, but everyone must give a big quiet clap (no sound!) at the end.
squares: START
Hum like a bee: what is shaking?
Whisper your name
Echo in a cave: go forward 2
Bark like a dog
Too loud! Cover your ears: miss a turn
Tap a table: does wood carry sound?
Roar like a tiger
Elephant rumble: say it as low as you can
Fireworks scared the birds: go back 2
Clap twice
String telephone works: go forward 2
Hiss like a snake
Name 3 sound sources in this room
No air in space: no sound! Mime a word
Click like a thirsty tomato plant
Drum on your knees
A loud speaker hurt your ears: go back 1
Sing one line of a song
Bat in the dark: squeak and go forward 1
Ring like a bicycle bell
HOME

big: Is there any place in the world that is completely silent?
If a tree falls in a forest and no one is there, does it make a sound?
Do animals hear the world the same way we do?
Which sounds do you love? Which sounds might frighten a dog or a bird?
If you tap it, shake it or listen closely enough, does everything make a sound?

challenge.q: In space films, spaceships blow up with a huge BANG. Is that true?
challenge.hint: Space has almost no air, so there is nothing to carry the shake. A real explosion in space would be silent. Astronauts talk by radio. Ask: why do you think film makers add the bang?

challenge.q: People say 'blind as a bat'. Are bats blind?
challenge.hint: No bat is blind. Many see well, and fruit bats see very well. Insect-eating bats also use echoes of their own squeaks to find food in the dark. Ask: why might people have thought bats could not see?

challenge.q: If you shout, does your voice travel faster than if you whisper?
challenge.hint: No. A shout is louder, so it can be heard further away, but loud and quiet sounds travel through air at the same speed. Ask: how could you test this with a friend far away?

perspectives.who: A blind or visually impaired person
perspectives.view: Many blind people know a great deal from sound: how big a room is, where a wall is, whether a road is busy. Some click their tongues and listen to the echoes, like bats. Ask: close your eyes in a room and clap. Can you tell if it is big or small?

perspectives.who: A dog on a cracker night
perspectives.view: Dogs hear quiet and high sounds that we cannot, so crackers may sound even more frightening to them. Many dogs hide under beds when crackers go off at Deepavali. Ask: whose festival is it, and could we celebrate in a way that is kind to animals too?
A drummer tightens or loosens the skin to change the sound, and listens very carefully. Ask: can you make a higher sound on your rice drum by pulling the cling film tighter?

In Bhramari, the humming bee breath, people hum with their ears closed and feel the sound inside their own heads. Many people say it calms them. Ask: when you hum with your ears closed, where is the sound: outside you or inside you?

story.title: Lakhi Listens with Her Feet
text: I am Lakhi, and I am an elephant, and when this happened I was very small: only as tall as a buffalo, with a trunk that still got in my way.

My family lived where the grass grows taller than a house. In the mornings the mist lies on it like a white blanket, and the grass stalks are wet and sharp and smell of rain. My mother walked in front of me, and my aunts walked around me, and my grandmother, who was the oldest and the biggest and knew every path, walked in front of us all.

That morning I saw a butterfly. They were yellow, as yellow as a ripe mango, and they floated just in front of my trunk. I reached for them. They floated away. I followed. I reached again. They floated further, between the grass stalks, and I pushed after them, and they went up and up into the sky, and were gone.
When I turned round, there was only grass.

Grass in front of me. Grass behind me. Grass on both sides, tall and green and swaying, so that I could not see anything but grass and a little piece of grey sky. I could not see my mother's big grey legs. I could not see my aunts. I could not see my grandmother.
I lifted my trunk and trumpeted as loud as I could. My trumpet was small and squeaky, and the grass swallowed it up.
I listened. A bird called, far away. The grass hissed in the wind. Somewhere, water was running. But no elephant called back.
My heart beat very fast. I started to run, this way, then that way, and the sharp grass scratched my sides, and every way looked the same. I stopped, and my legs shook.
And then I remembered something my grandmother had told me.
It was on a quiet evening by the river. I had asked her, “Grandmother, how do you always know where everyone is, even when they are far away behind the trees?”

She had rumbled, low and slow, so low that I felt it more than I heard it. It tickled the inside of my chest. “Little one,” she said, “we elephants talk with a voice so deep that it goes a long, long way. It goes through the air, and it goes through the ground too. Your ears hear some of it. But your feet hear the rest.”
“My feet?” I had laughed. “Feet can't hear!”
“Try,” said Grandmother. “When you are lost, do not run. Running makes your feet noisy. Stand still. Put your feet flat. Lay your trunk on the ground. And wait.”
So now, in the tall grass, with my heart beating like a drum, I made myself stop.
I stood still. I pressed my four feet flat into the soft wet earth. I laid the tip of my trunk on the ground. I waited. The bird called. The grass hissed. I waited.
And then I felt it.

It was not a sound, not exactly. It was a shiver in the ground. It came up through the soles of my feet, a slow, deep trembling, like the ground itself was humming. It came again. It was stronger in my front left foot than my back right foot, so I turned a little that way, and then it was the same in both front feet.

I knew that trembling. It was my grandmother's rumble, the one that tickled my chest by the river. She was calling me, low and deep, and her call was shaking the earth all the way from where she stood to where I stood.

I walked towards it. Every few steps I stopped, stood still and felt again, and every time the trembling was a little bigger. The grass was still tall. I still could not see. But I was not lost any more, because I could feel which way my family was.

Then the grass opened, and there was a great grey leg, and another, and my mother's trunk came down and wrapped around me, and my aunts were rumbling and flapping their ears, and the ground was full of their voices.
My grandmother did not say anything at first. She just touched the top of my head with the tip of her trunk.
Then she rumbled, very softly, so that I felt it in my feet: “You stood still.”
Now I am big, and I have a little one of my own, who also chases butterflies. And on quiet evenings by the river, I tell her what my grandmother told me. She laughs, just like I did.
But one day, I think, she will stand still in the tall grass, and press her feet into the earth, and feel the ground hum.
story.epiphany: A sound is a shake that travels, through the air and also through the ground. Elephants make very low rumbles that travel far and can be felt through their feet and trunks. The turn comes when Lakhi stops running, stands still and feels the trembling, and uses which foot feels it most to find the way.
ask: How did Lakhi find her family when she could not see them or hear them?
Why did Grandmother say 'do not run, stand still'?
Can you feel a sound with your body? When have you felt one?
Why do you think Lakhi's squeaky trumpet did not reach her family, but Grandmother's low rumble did?
How do you think Lakhi felt when she was lost, and when she was found?

ideas.idea: Every sound in the world starts with a shake.
ideas.more: A voice box, a drum skin, a guitar string, a bee's wings: something always vibrates. Stop the shake and the sound stops. Touch a ringing steel glass to show it.

ideas.idea: Sound is a vibration passed along from one bit of air to the next.
ideas.more: The air next to a drum pushes the air beside it, and that air pushes the next, all the way to your ear. Nothing flies from the drum to you. That is why sound needs air, water, wood or string to travel through. Ripples in a plate of water show the same thing: the wave spreads while the water stays in place.

ideas.idea: Other animals live in a different world of sound.
ideas.more: Elephants talk below what we can hear, bats and dolphins far above it, and dogs hear quiet sounds we miss. Our ears catch only a small part of all the sounds there are.

unknowns: Do any animals listen to the tiny clicks that thirsty plants make? Nobody knows yet.
How much do elephants understand from the rumbles they feel in the ground? Can they tell who is calling, and what they are saying? Scientists are still finding out.
Why do some sounds, like a lullaby or rain, make us feel calm, while others make us feel scared? Scientists do not fully understand how the brain does this.

check.q: What is a sound source? Name three.
check.a: Anything that makes a sound, for example a crow, a pressure cooker and rain on the roof.

check.q: What happens to something when it makes a sound?
check.a: It vibrates, which means it shakes very fast.

check.q: What happens to a sound as you walk away from it?
check.a: It gets quieter, because the shake spreads out and gets weaker.

check.q: Name three things sound can travel through.
Why should we never put anything inside our ears?
check.a: The eardrum is thin and can be hurt.
